rows.description: Recognizing personal strengths and needs, such as attention, dyslexia or sensory sensitivity, and asking for support.
Building workplace and life systems that fit one's own attention, sensory and energy patterns.

rows.subtype: Quick cycles of try, check, adjust [Response]
rows.description: A capable maker builds a small version, tests it, learns what is wrong and revises, repeating many times. Short loops turn mistakes into cheap information rather than costly disasters.

rows.subtype: Giving feedback that can be used [Response]
rows.description: A wise reviewer names what works, points to a concrete spot that needs change, and says why. Specific, timely, kind feedback lets the receiver act on it instead of defending.
A child drums fingers or fidgets from boredom, energy or focus. Watching for context, since fidgeting may help concentration, prevents unfair scolding.
A child snaps the fingers in rhythm or to call attention, and rubs the hands from cold or eager anticipation. Meaning depends on context, and snapping at people can seem rude.

rows.subtype: Rubbing hands and drumming at work [Mismatch]
rows.description: A colleague rubs the hands in anticipation or drums the fingers in impatience, and it can be either. Asking about it works better than guessing.
A child who lost a game cries, is comforted and then tries again; resilience begins with a warm relationship that makes hard feelings safe.
A student who failed a paper acknowledges the disappointment, then asks what it tells them about preparation; the reframe keeps honesty and opens options.

rows.subtype: Problem solving one piece at a time [Response]
rows.description: An adult facing a job loss lists tasks, picks the first and does it; breaking a huge threat into steps restores a sense of control.
A child sees how relatives treat a parent with a senior post differently from one in a small job, and absorbs that work equals rank. Adults can teach that honest work of any kind carries dignity.
A junior watches a senior invite disagreement and thank the person who raised it, and feels safe to speak. Such leaders build honest teams and are remembered kindly for decades.

A child pressing lips together to hold back a smile after a mischief or a funny remark is trying to control amusement or pride. It usually shows the child knows the social rule, and it often leaks through the eyes.

A teenager keeps a slight smile at school while feeling low, to avoid questions. Trusted adults can notice a smile that does not reach the eyes or fits poorly with other cues, and offer a gentle open door without pressure.

rows.subtype: Broad smile as customer or leadership tool [Regulating]
rows.description: A young professional uses a broad, open-mouth smile to set clients at ease or to open a meeting. It works best when it matches honest goodwill, and habitual smiling over real worry can wear a person down.
